title: Public education and misinformation on brain death in mainstream media
screen_reason: Content analysis of 208 unique mainstream-media articles about the Jahi McMath and Marlise Munoz brain-death cases, published on the eight most-trafficked US news sites before 31 July 2015. Each article was coded by a neurointensivist for whether it contained misinformation, explicitly defined by the authors and judged against established medical and legal facts about brain death. The paper reports 'Misinformation was present in 74% (154) of the articles', a share of items in a sample judged inaccurate against an external ground truth, so this is a CONTENT prevalence estimate. Flagged borderline because the authors' definition of misinformation includes 'incomplete' information, so an article that says nothing false can be counted.

estimates.platform: Mainstream media websites (eight of the ten most shared/heavily trafficked US news sites of 2014, per Pew)
estimates.date: Articles published before 31 July 2015; 87% published December 2013 to February 2014
estimates.measure_type: % of mainstream-media articles about two brain-death cases that contained misinformation about brain death
estimates.denominator: 208 unique articles retrieved by searching 'Jahi McMath' and 'Marlise Munoz' on eight most-trafficked US mainstream media websites (blogs, videos, photo stories and news briefs excluded)
estimates.definition: Article contained misleading, incomplete or incorrect information about brain death, including quoting an individual without pointing out why the quote was misleading, incomplete or incorrect, such that readers would inappropriately accept it as fact
estimates.misinfo_def: misinformation, defined as misleading, incomplete, or incorrect information including situations in which the author quoted an individual and did not point out why the quote was misleading, incomplete or incorrect such that readers would inappropriately accept the content of the quotes as facts
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation was present in 74% (154) of the articles.
estimates.page_loc: Results, first paragraph after the search yield (accepted manuscript, unpaginated)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: A single author (AL, a neurointensivist) reviewed and coded every article against key concepts about brain death drawn from major publications; a second author (ASL) recoded a random 10% for reliability, giving unweighted kappa = 0.578 (95% CI 0.462-0.694, p < 0.0005), described by the authors as moderate agreement.
estimates.moderator_quote: A list of the top ten most shared/heavily trafficked mainstream media websites of 2014 was obtained from the Pew Research Center.
estimates.notes: Borderline for two reasons. First, the case definition folds 'incomplete' into misinformation, so an article that contains no false statement but omits context can be counted; this is the failure mode where a wholly true item carries the label, and it is why breadth is coded misleading rather than false. Second, the reliability is only moderate (kappa 0.578) and coding was otherwise done by one author. The frame is two named cases on eight curated outlets, so the estimate is about coverage of brain death, not about news generally. Year set to 2015, the end of the article window; the paper was published in 2016.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) 'The subject was referred to by the author (not by the family) as being "alive" or on "life support" in 72% (149) of the articles, 97% (144) of which also described the subject as being brain dead' - the authors' own qualifier shows most of these articles also stated the subject was brain dead, so a factually correct article can carry this label; it is framing/word choice rather than a falsity verdict, and it overlaps heavily with the 74% headline; (b) '47% (16) of these implied there was no difference between a persistent vegetative state and brain death' - a genuine falsity judgement, but its denominator is only the 34 articles that mentioned Schiavo/Quinlan/Cruzan, i.e. a subset of a subset, and it is a component of the 74% headline rather than an independent estimate; extracting it would double-count; (c) the teaching-point and completeness figures (29% referenced legal/medical/social facts, 4% defined brain death, 2% mentioned the Uniform Determination of Death Act, 7% noted organ support should be discontinued, 5% on physician permission) - omission measures, not veracity, and the paper's own framing of them is 'education' rather than misinformation; (d) per-site teaching-point shares (Washington Post 71%, Daily Mail 28%, NY Times 37%) and per-period shares (31%, 23%, 48%) - subgroup splits of a quality measure, not the headline. One thing a human should note: the 74% misinformation figure and the 72% 'alive/life support' figure are close enough that they may be near-coextensive, but the paper never says how much the categories overlap.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. Frame: the ten most shared/heavily trafficked US mainstream media websites of 2014 per Pew, minus two aggregator sites, searched for 'Jahi McMath' and 'Marlise Munoz'; all articles published before 31 July 2015 reviewed, blogs, videos, photo stories and news briefs excluded, duplicates removed by title and text comparison; 208 unique articles on eight sites (141 McMath, 61 Munoz, 6 both). Coding by one author into a RedCap instrument designed by all authors, with 10% randomly recoded by a second author; unweighted kappa 0.578 (95% CI 0.462-0.694). Descriptive statistics only. No IRB required.
rob.item6_quote: The data for each article was evaluated (AL) to determine whether the article contained 1) teaching points (see Table 1), or 2) misinformation, defined as misleading, incomplete, or incorrect
rob.item10_quote: Misinformation was present in 74% (154) of the articles.
